name: Plural -s

1.specialization: Realizes plural number on an eligible nominal stem

2.specialization: Realizes plural number when the noun is used to count types or varieties

3.specialization: Realizes plural number in a construction that describes recurring instances

4.specialization: Forms common nouns denoting groups from proper nouns used as names

projection.target: With transparent regular plural formation, the final sound of the stem predicts the suffix pronunciation. Compare the /s/ in cats, /z/ in dogs, and /ɪz/ in horses. A variety interpretation additionally depends on count use of the noun.
projection.evidence: CGEL describes the sibilant allomorphy and separately documents contextual count readings.

curious.title: Adding -s to make a plural
curious.summary: Adding -s or -es to a common noun makes it plural, and the same ending can also count types, repeated events or members of a family.
curious.body:
The ending -s turns cat into cats, marking more than one. The ending is pronounced differently depending on the last sound of the word: an s sound in cats, a z sound in dogs, and an extra syllable, like iz, in horses.

The same ending does other jobs. Wines counts types of wine. I get headaches describes headaches that come back. And the Kennedys names the members of a family or dynasty, built from a name. Which job the ending does depends on how the noun is being used.
curious.try: Say cats, dogs and horses aloud. Can you hear the three different endings?

teacher.summary: Covers regular plural -s/-es, its pronunciation, and its extensions to types, recurring instances and family names.
teacher.explain: Plural -s or -es attaches to a common-noun stem and realizes plural number. In regular formation the final sound of the stem predicts the pronunciation of the suffix: /s/ in cats, /z/ in dogs, /ɪz/ in horses. The same suffix realizes plural number in several uses: non-singular (cats), types or varieties of a substance (wines), recurring instances (I get headaches), and groups formed from proper names (the Kennedys, meaning Kennedy family or dynasty members). A variety reading depends on the noun being used as a count noun. This dictionary marks this as provisional, with medium confidence.
teacher.terms: The sibilant ending is sometimes called an allomorph of the plural suffix.

contrasts.note: Three pronunciations of one suffix, set by the last sound of the stem.

watch_for: A learner might pronounce the ending the same way in cats, dogs and horses.
A learner might read wines only as more than one bottle, when it can count types of wine.
teacher.activity: Students sort a list of plural nouns by the ending sound (s, z, iz) and say what the last sound of the singular is each time.

child.hook: Does the s on cats sound the same as the s on dogs?
child.explain: Adding s to a word can mean more than one. Cats ends with an s sound. Dogs ends with a z sound. Horses ends with an extra bit, like iz.
child.play: Say a list of plural words aloud. Sort them by the ending you hear: s, z or iz.
